LPA-CWM: A Learned Physical Adjudicator
for Motion Reasoning with Counterfactual World Models

Kunwei Wu1,* Xiang Liu2,* Guocai Yao3 Junming Chen4 Zhikang Chen5 Min Zhang6 Pengwei Wang3 Sen Cui2,†\dagger
1National University of Singapore 2Tsinghua University 3Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence 4Facebook 5University of Oxford 6East China Normal University
*Equal contribution   †\daggerProject Leader & Corresponding Author
Contact: wukunwei@u.nus.edu |  xiang-liu25@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn |  cuis@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn
Abstract

Counterfactual world models (CWM) extract motion from pretrained video predictors by comparing factual and intervened predictions. However, responses generated under different target-frame masks vary in reliability, while uniform aggregation weights them equally. We formulate response aggregation as candidate reliability learning and propose LPA-CWM with a lightweight Learned Physical Adjudicator (LPA). Trained on dense MOVi-F trajectories, the 3.0M-parameter LPA compares visual context and response structure across an unordered candidate set to predict relative weights, while the CWM predictor and intervention generator remain frozen. The weighted responses undergo windowed localization and one paired re-evaluation to recover motion. We also introduce Completeness-aware Motion Correspondence (CMC), a ground-truth-anchored evaluation protocol that jointly measures localization, trajectory completeness, visibility, and continuity, counting missing predictions as failures on visible dynamic points. On the evaluated DAVIS and Kinetics subsets, LPA-CWM improves DCAavg\mathrm{DCA}_{\mathrm{avg}} over Uniform CWM by 60.0% and 29.0%, respectively, and also improves tracking accuracy under TAP-Vid First. A quick overview is available at https://LPA-CWM.github.io.

   

1 Introduction

World models learn predictive representations of visual dynamics (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019; Hafner et al., 2020). Counterfactual World Modeling (CWM) extracts motion from these representations by comparing predictions with and without localized interventions (Bear et al., 2023; Venkatesh et al., 2024; Stojanov et al., 2025). Different target-frame masks can produce inconsistent responses for the same query: some localize the motion well, while others are affected by background content, competing motion, or visual ambiguity. Uniform aggregation treats all responses as equally reliable and can dilute useful evidence. This raises two questions: how should counterfactual motion evidence be combined, and how should the recovered trajectories be evaluated?

To improve CWM inference, we formulate multi-mask aggregation as candidate reliability estimation. We first derive APA-CWM, an Analytic Physical Adjudicator (APA) from the Normalized Spatiotemporal Gradient (NSG) (Zhang et al., 2025). APA reads the NSG-derived spatiotemporal consistency around each candidate response peak and converts these local scores into closed-form reliability weights. It provides a training-free physical reference for testing how far an analytic consistency prior can resolve candidate ambiguity. We then propose LPA-CWM, whose Learned Physical Adjudicator (LPA) combines local visual evidence, response morphology, shared frame-pair context, and candidate statistics. A Transformer without candidate-index positional embeddings jointly compares the unordered candidate set and predicts relative weights.

We train only the 3.0M-parameter LPA on dense Kubric MOVi-F trajectories (Greff et al., 2022). For each query, dense forward motion provides the oracle target endpoint; candidate endpoint errors define relative reliability targets and supervise distribution matching, weighted-coordinate localization, and best-candidate ranking. This gives direct supervision for which CWM responses are trustworthy while leaving the pretrained CWM unchanged. At inference, LPA weights the initial responses, followed by windowed localization and one paired CWM re-evaluation to obtain the final motion.

Existing benchmarks assess video quality, temporal consistency, physical and commonsense faithfulness, controllability, embodied utility, and counterfactual consistency (Huang et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025; Duan et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2026; Begiristain et al., 2026). They broaden evaluation beyond visual plausibility, but do not directly measure point correspondence recovered through CWM interventions. In motion recovery, low error on returned predictions can hide missing trajectory segments, while smooth trajectories may still follow incorrect motion.

We therefore introduce Completeness-aware Motion Correspondence (CMC), a ground-truth-anchored protocol built on TAP-Vid annotations (Doersch et al., 2022). CMC evaluates localization, completeness, visibility, and temporal continuity on dynamic point tracks. Dynamic Correspondence Accuracy requires visible predictions within a distance threshold and counts missing predictions as failures on ground-truth-visible points. Track-level success further requires sufficient coverage and bounded localization error, while visibility and continuity diagnostics expose interrupted trajectories. CMC complements TAP-Vid First by making completeness on moving tracks an explicit target.

We evaluate on DAVIS and Kinetics (Pont-Tuset et al., 2017; Kay et al., 2017) against SMURF, GMRW, DODUO, CoTracker3, RAFT, and SEA-RAFT, covering self-supervised flow, global correspondence, dense optical flow, and dedicated point tracking (Stone et al., 2021; Shrivastava and Owens, 2024; Jiang et al., 2024; Karaev et al., 2025; Teed and Deng, 2020; Wang et al., 2024). LPA-CWM improves DCAavg\mathrm{DCA}_{\mathrm{avg}} over Uniform CWM by 60.0% on DAVIS and 29.0% on Kinetics. On Kinetics it achieves the best value across all reported CMC metrics; on DAVIS it gives the highest coverage, Complete@0.8, and continuity, while CoTracker3 remains stronger on several conventional tracking measures. Within the CWM family, LPA-CWM also improves all TAP-Vid First measures over Uniform CWM and APA-CWM.

In summary, our main contributions are:

  • •

    We formulate multi-mask CWM inference as candidate reliability estimation and introduce analytic and learned reliability weighting for counterfactual motion responses.

  • •

    We propose LPA-CWM, a lightweight physically supervised adjudicator trained from dense MOVi-F trajectories, with windowed localization and one paired CWM re-evaluation.

  • •

    We introduce CMC for joint evaluation of localization, completeness, visibility, and continuity, and show strong gains over Uniform CWM, APA-CWM, and external baselines.

2 Related Work

World models and counterfactual motion.

Video world models learn predictive representations through feature prediction, as in V-JEPA (Bardes et al., 2024), or action-controllable generation, as in Genie (Bruce et al., 2024). CWM extracts correspondence by comparing factual and locally intervened predictions (Bear et al., 2023), and later work applies this interface to physical dynamics (Venkatesh et al., 2024). Opt-CWM learns query-conditioned perturbations for flow and occlusion (Stojanov et al., 2025); KL-tracing measures the response of generative video models through KL divergence (Kim et al., 2025); and Point Prompting propagates colored markers through video diffusion models (Shrivastava et al., 2026). LPA-CWM focuses on learning the relative reliability of the multiple responses already produced by a frozen CWM.

Diffusion models as structural priors.

Diffusion features also support visual correspondence. SD4Match adapts Stable Diffusion features with image-pair-conditioned prompts (Li et al., 2024), while Track4Gen jointly trains video generation and point correspondence to reduce appearance drift (Jeong et al., 2025). NSG relates a diffusion score field to observed inter-frame changes as a spatiotemporal consistency signal (Zhang et al., 2025). APA-CWM uses this signal for analytic candidate weighting, while LPA-CWM learns the weights from trajectory supervision.

Flow, correspondence, and point tracking.

Our external baselines cover complementary motion interfaces. RAFT uses all-pairs correlations with iterative flow refinement (Teed and Deng, 2020), and SEA-RAFT improves the framework with probabilistic training and a more efficient design (Wang et al., 2024). SMURF learns optical flow through full-image warping and multi-frame self-supervision (Stone et al., 2021). GMRW learns global correspondence with contrastive random walks (Shrivastava and Owens, 2024), whereas DODUO combines semantic priors with self-supervised flow (Jiang et al., 2024). CoTracker3 is a dedicated point tracker trained with pseudo-labels from real videos (Karaev et al., 2025); AllTracker extends dense long-range tracking with multi-frame flow and temporal attention (Harley et al., 2025).

Evaluation of motion consistency.

General video and world-model benchmarks measure complementary properties: VBench targets visual quality and temporal consistency (Huang et al., 2024), VBench-2.0 adds physical and commonsense faithfulness (Zheng et al., 2025), WorldScore evaluates controllability, quality, and dynamics (Duan et al., 2025), WorldArena includes embodied task utility (Shang et al., 2026), and CRONOS tests counterfactual physical consistency (Begiristain et al., 2026). Motion-specific evaluation includes FVMD for point-track motion distributions (Liu et al., 2024), Physics-IQ for prediction against real physical experiments (Motamed et al., 2026), and TAPVid-3D for long-range 3D correspondence and visibility (Koppula et al., 2024). CMC instead evaluates recovered 2D dynamic tracks, counting missing visible predictions as failures and reporting completeness and continuity alongside localization.

3 Method

Given two consecutive frames and a query point, our method first uses a frozen counterfactual world model (CWM) to produce multiple motion candidates. We then compare two ways to weight these candidates: an analytic rule, APA-CWM, and a learned adjudicator, LPA-CWM. Both variants combine the candidate response maps before applying the same localization and re-evaluation procedure. Figure 2 summarizes the method.

3.1 Counterfactual Motion Candidates from a Frozen World Model

Let 𝐈t,𝐈t+1∈[0,1]256×256×3\mathbf{I}_{t},\mathbf{I}_{t+1}\in[0,1]^{256\times 256\times 3} be two consecutive RGB frames, and let 𝐩t∈Ω\mathbf{p}_{t}\in\Omega be a query location in the first frame, where Ω\Omega is the 256×256256\times 256 image grid. We build on counterfactual world models (Bear et al., 2023; Venkatesh et al., 2024; Stojanov et al., 2025), consisting of an RGB predictor ΨRGB\Psi^{\mathrm{RGB}} and a query-conditioned intervention generator 𝜹θ\bm{\delta}_{\theta}. Both ΨRGB\Psi^{\mathrm{RGB}} and 𝜹θ\bm{\delta}_{\theta} are pretrained and remain fixed.

The generator produces the intervention 𝜹t=𝜹θ​(𝐈t,𝐩t)∈ℝ256×256×3\bm{\delta}_{t}=\bm{\delta}_{\theta}(\mathbf{I}_{t},\mathbf{p}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{256\times 256\times 3}. For each target-frame mask ℳm\mathcal{M}_{m}, CWM measures how this intervention changes the target prediction:

𝚫m=ΨRGB​(𝐈t+𝜹t,ℳm​(𝐈t+1))−ΨRGB​(𝐈t,ℳm​(𝐈t+1)).\bm{\Delta}_{m}=\Psi^{\mathrm{RGB}}\!\left(\mathbf{I}_{t}+\bm{\delta}_{t},\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbf{I}_{t+1})\right)-\Psi^{\mathrm{RGB}}\!\left(\mathbf{I}_{t},\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbf{I}_{t+1})\right). (1)

Thus, 𝚫m​(𝐮)\bm{\Delta}_{m}(\mathbf{u}) measures how much the prediction at target pixel 𝐮\mathbf{u} changes when the source query is intervened. A large response indicates a strong dependency between that target location and the queried source region. Repeating this process for MM masks produces

𝒞t={𝚫m,𝐩^t+1(m)}m=1M,𝐩^t+1(m)=arg⁡max𝐮∈Ω⁡‖𝚫m​(𝐮)‖1.\mathcal{C}_{t}=\left\{\bm{\Delta}_{m},\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{t+1}^{(m)}\right\}_{m=1}^{M},\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{t+1}^{(m)}=\arg\max_{\mathbf{u}\in\Omega}\left\|\bm{\Delta}_{m}(\mathbf{u})\right\|_{1}. (2)

Here, 𝐮\mathbf{u} indexes target-frame pixels and the ℓ1\ell_{1} norm reduces the three RGB channels. The peak 𝐩^t+1(m)\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{t+1}^{(m)} is the target location with the strongest response under mask mm, and therefore serves as that mask’s proposed endpoint for the query 𝐩t\mathbf{p}_{t}. Because different masks expose different target contexts, their response maps and candidate endpoints can disagree. Uniform CWM averages all responses equally, whereas APA-CWM and LPA-CWM estimate candidate-specific weights.

3.2 Analytic Candidate Weighting

APA-CWM provides a closed-form reference based on the Normalized Spatiotemporal Gradient (NSG) (Zhang et al., 2025). Let 𝐱t,𝐱t+1∈[−1,1]224×224×3\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\in[-1,1]^{224\times 224\times 3} denote the frame pair (𝐈t,𝐈t+1)(\mathbf{I}_{t},\mathbf{I}_{t+1}) after preprocessing for a frozen Ablated Diffusion Model (ADM) (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021). The notation distinguishes these ADM inputs from the 256×256256\times 256 RGB frames used by CWM. Let 𝐬ϕ\mathbf{s}_{\phi} be the frozen ADM score network, tst_{s} its diffusion time, and 𝐮\mathbf{u} a location on the ADM grid.

Following NSG, we compute a spatial score 𝒫\mathcal{P} that compares the local ADM score magnitude with its alignment to the observed frame change:

𝒫⁡(𝐮)=‖𝐬ϕ​(𝐱t,ts)​(𝐮)‖2|⟨𝐬ϕ​(𝐱t,ts)​(𝐮),𝐱t+1​(𝐮)−𝐱t​(𝐮)⟩|+10−6.\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{u})=\frac{\left\|\mathbf{s}_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t_{s})(\mathbf{u})\right\|_{2}}{\left|\left\langle\mathbf{s}_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t_{s})(\mathbf{u}),\mathbf{x}_{t+1}(\mathbf{u})-\mathbf{x}_{t}(\mathbf{u})\right\rangle\right|+10^{-6}}. (3)

The numerator measures the local score magnitude, while the denominator measures its projection onto the observed inter-frame change. The constant 10−610^{-6} prevents numerical instability when this inner product is close to zero. APA treats the resulting 𝒫\mathcal{P} map as a local physical consistency cue for judging the CWM candidates.

We bilinearly resize 𝒫\mathcal{P} to the CWM response grid and keep the same notation for the aligned map. For each candidate, APA averages this score in the radius-six neighborhood 𝒩6\mathcal{N}_{6} around its response peak and then normalizes the candidate scores:

rmAPA=1|𝒩6​(𝐩^t+1(m))|​∑𝐮∈𝒩6​(𝐩^t+1(m))𝒫⁡(𝐮),wmAPA=clip⁡(rmAPA,10−3,103)∑jclip⁡(rjAPA,10−3,103).r_{m}^{\mathrm{APA}}=\frac{1}{\left|\mathcal{N}_{6}(\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{t+1}^{(m)})\right|}\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{N}_{6}(\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{t+1}^{(m)})}\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{u}),\qquad w_{m}^{\mathrm{APA}}=\frac{\operatorname{clip}(r_{m}^{\mathrm{APA}},10^{-3},10^{3})}{\sum_{j}\operatorname{clip}(r_{j}^{\mathrm{APA}},10^{-3},10^{3})}. (4)

Here, rmAPAr_{m}^{\mathrm{APA}} is the local NSG score for candidate mm. Clipping limits extreme values, and normalization converts these scores into nonnegative candidate weights wmAPAw_{m}^{\mathrm{APA}} that sum to one. APA thus provides a training-free way to favor candidates supported by the NSG cue. Since this cue is not directly supervised by endpoint accuracy, we next learn candidate reliability from dense motion trajectories.

3.3 Learned Physical Adjudicator

Candidate representation and set reasoning.

LPA represents each candidate using four sources of information. (1) Local visual evidence: the local branch receives a 10-channel 32×3232\times 32 tensor containing source and target RGB crops, their absolute RGB difference, and a crop of the candidate response. These inputs correspond to 64×6464\times 64 regions centered at 𝐩t\mathbf{p}_{t} and 𝐩^t+1(m)\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{t+1}^{(m)}. Before cropping, the RGB response is reduced and normalized as d~m​(𝐮)=‖𝚫m​(𝐮)‖1/(max𝐯⁡‖𝚫m​(𝐯)‖1+10−8)\widetilde{d}_{m}(\mathbf{u})=\|\bm{\Delta}_{m}(\mathbf{u})\|_{1}/(\max_{\mathbf{v}}\|\bm{\Delta}_{m}(\mathbf{v})\|_{1}+10^{-8}). (2) Full response: a second branch encodes the complete d~m\widetilde{d}_{m} map to retain the global shape and ambiguity of the response. (3) Frame context: a third branch encodes the full frame pair to provide scene-level visual information shared by all candidates. (4) Candidate statistics: the final branch encodes 16 scalar descriptors covering displacement, response concentration, ambiguity, photometric change, and edge strength. The exact descriptors and encoder architectures are given in Appendix A.

The four encoded features are combined and projected to a 256-dimensional candidate token 𝐳m\mathbf{z}_{m}. We denote the Transformer encoder without candidate-order embeddings by SetEnc\operatorname{SetEnc}. It compares all candidate tokens, after which a shared scoring head hscoreh_{\mathrm{score}} produces one score per candidate:

[𝐳~1,…,𝐳~M]=SetEnc⁡([𝐳1,…,𝐳M]),wmLPA=exp⁡(hscore​(𝐳~m))∑jexp⁡(hscore​(𝐳~j)).\left[\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{M}\right]=\operatorname{SetEnc}\left([\mathbf{z}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{z}_{M}]\right),\qquad w_{m}^{\mathrm{LPA}}=\frac{\exp(h_{\mathrm{score}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{m}))}{\sum_{j}\exp(h_{\mathrm{score}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{j}))}. (5)

The softmax converts these scores into normalized LPA weights wmLPAw_{m}^{\mathrm{LPA}}. Without candidate-order embeddings, permuting the input candidates only permutes their output weights, while the weighted response remains unchanged. We also randomize candidate order during training.

Dense-trajectory supervision.

We train LPA on M=10M=10 candidate sets generated from adjacent MOVi-F frames (Greff et al., 2022); training and validation videos are disjoint. MOVi-F provides a dense ground-truth forward motion field 𝐅t→t+1\mathbf{F}_{t\rightarrow t+1}, where 𝐅t→t+1​(𝐩t)\mathbf{F}_{t\rightarrow t+1}(\mathbf{p}_{t}) is the displacement of 𝐩t\mathbf{p}_{t} from frame tt to t+1t+1. The corresponding ground-truth endpoint is 𝐩t+1∗=𝐩t+𝐅t→t+1​(𝐩t)\mathbf{p}_{t+1}^{*}=\mathbf{p}_{t}+\mathbf{F}_{t\rightarrow t+1}(\mathbf{p}_{t}).

We use this endpoint to measure how reliable each candidate is. Specifically, eme_{m} is the endpoint error of candidate mm, and these errors are converted into a soft reliability target 𝐪=(q1,…,qM)\mathbf{q}=(q_{1},\ldots,q_{M}):

em=‖𝐩^t+1(m)−𝐩t+1∗‖2,qm=exp(−em/τq)∑jexp(−ej/τq),τq=4.e_{m}=\left\|\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{t+1}^{(m)}-\mathbf{p}_{t+1}^{*}\right\|_{2},\qquad q_{m}=\frac{\exp(-e_{m}/\tau_{q})}{\sum_{j}\exp(-e_{j}/\tau_{q})},\qquad\tau_{q}=4. (6)

Candidates closer to the ground-truth endpoint receive larger qmq_{m}. Unlike a hard label that selects only the single best candidate, 𝐪\mathbf{q} retains the relative quality of all candidates. The temperature τq\tau_{q} controls how strongly the target distribution favors candidates with lower endpoint error.

Training objective.

We train LPA with the following objective:

ℒ=DKL(𝐪∥𝐰LPA)+λ1SmoothL1(∑mwmLPA𝐩^t+1(m),𝐩t+1∗)+λ2CE(𝐚,argminmem),\mathcal{L}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mathbf{q}\|\mathbf{w}^{\mathrm{LPA}}\right)+\lambda_{1}\operatorname{SmoothL1}\!\left(\sum_{m}w_{m}^{\mathrm{LPA}}\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{t+1}^{(m)},\mathbf{p}_{t+1}^{*}\right)+\lambda_{2}\operatorname{CE}\!\left(\mathbf{a},\arg\min_{m}e_{m}\right), (7)

where 𝐚={hscore​(𝐳~m)}m=1M\mathbf{a}=\left\{h_{\mathrm{score}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{m})\right\}_{m=1}^{M} denotes the pre-softmax scores. The KL term matches the predicted weights to the soft reliability targets 𝐪\mathbf{q}. The SmoothL1 term encourages the weighted candidate endpoint toward the ground-truth endpoint, while the cross-entropy term encourages the lowest-error candidate to receive the highest score. In our experiments, we set λ1=2\lambda_{1}=2 and λ2=0.2\lambda_{2}=0.2.

The weighted candidate endpoint in the SmoothL1 term is used only as a differentiable training signal. During inference, LPA does not directly average candidate peak coordinates; instead, its predicted weights are applied to the full CWM response maps, which are then decoded as described next. MOVi-F correspondence filtering and further training details are given in Appendix A.

3.4 Weighted Aggregation and Localized Decoding

Weighted response aggregation.

Let wmw_{m} denote the uniform, analytic, or learned candidate weight used by Uniform CWM, APA-CWM, or LPA-CWM, respectively. We first combine the full candidate responses and reduce the three RGB channels to a scalar localization map:

𝚫¯w=∑m=1Mwm​𝚫m,d¯w​(𝐮)=13​‖𝚫¯w​(𝐮)‖1,wm≥0,∑mwm=1.\overline{\bm{\Delta}}_{w}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}w_{m}\bm{\Delta}_{m},\qquad\overline{d}_{w}(\mathbf{u})=\frac{1}{3}\left\|\overline{\bm{\Delta}}_{w}(\mathbf{u})\right\|_{1},\qquad w_{m}\geq 0,\quad\sum_{m}w_{m}=1. (8)

Here, 𝚫¯w\overline{\bm{\Delta}}_{w} is the weighted CWM response and d¯w​(𝐮)\overline{d}_{w}(\mathbf{u}) measures its response strength at pixel 𝐮\mathbf{u}. Larger values indicate locations more strongly supported by the aggregated candidates.

Windowed localization and re-evaluation.

To locate the endpoint, we turn d¯w\overline{d}_{w} into a normalized spatial distribution π(0)​(𝐮)∝exp⁡(βπ​d¯w​(𝐮))\pi^{(0)}(\mathbf{u})\propto\exp(\beta_{\pi}\overline{d}_{w}(\mathbf{u})), with βπ=200\beta_{\pi}=200, normalized over all 𝐮∈Ω\mathbf{u}\in\Omega. Thus, π(0)​(𝐮)\pi^{(0)}(\mathbf{u}) gives the relative support for pixel 𝐮\mathbf{u} as the endpoint, while π(k)\pi^{(k)} denotes this distribution after kk windowing updates. Standard localization directly selects the peak of π(0)\pi^{(0)}; our windowed localization instead applies two updates to suppress distant secondary peaks.

At each update, we compute the spatial mean 𝝁(k)\bm{\mu}^{(k)} and spread σ(k)\sigma^{(k)} of the current distribution, then apply a Gaussian window centered on the dominant region:

{𝝁(k)=∑𝐮π(k)​(𝐮)​𝐮,σ(k)=[∑𝐮π(k)​(𝐮)​‖𝐮−𝝁(k)‖22]1/2,π(k+1)​(𝐮)∝π(k)​(𝐮)​exp⁡[−‖𝐮−𝝁(k)‖222​[3​max⁡(σ(k),0.5)]2].\begin{cases}\bm{\mu}^{(k)}=\sum_{\mathbf{u}}\pi^{(k)}(\mathbf{u})\mathbf{u},\\ \sigma^{(k)}=\left[\sum_{\mathbf{u}}\pi^{(k)}(\mathbf{u})\left\|\mathbf{u}-\bm{\mu}^{(k)}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]^{1/2},\\ \pi^{(k+1)}(\mathbf{u})\propto\pi^{(k)}(\mathbf{u})\exp\!\left[-\frac{\left\|\mathbf{u}-\bm{\mu}^{(k)}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2[3\max(\sigma^{(k)},0.5)]^{2}}\right].\end{cases} (9)

Each update preserves the main response region while reducing the influence of distant modes. The window scale follows the current response spread, while max⁡(σ(k),0.5)\max(\sigma^{(k)},0.5) prevents it from collapsing when the distribution becomes highly concentrated. We apply this update twice as our inference setting. The pixel with the largest value in π(2)\pi^{(2)} is taken as the initial endpoint.

Finally, this initial endpoint determines the target-mask center for one fresh, full-field CWM evaluation, while the source query remains 𝐩t\mathbf{p}_{t}. The new MM responses are averaged uniformly and decoded to obtain the refined endpoint 𝐩^t+1\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{t+1}; APA and LPA are not run again, and their initial weights are not reused. The pairwise motion is ϕ^t=𝐩^t+1−𝐩t\widehat{\bm{\phi}}_{t}=\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{t+1}-\mathbf{p}_{t}, and the refined endpoint becomes the query for the next frame pair. Visibility is inherited from the original CWM response-strength signal; LPA introduces no separate visibility head. Further decoding details are provided in Appendix A.

4 Experiments

Our experiments mainly address three questions: (1) Does learned candidate weighting improve motion recovered from a frozen CWM? (2) How does LPA-CWM compare with analytic weighting and external motion baselines under CMC and standard point-tracking evaluation? (3) Which components and weighting behaviors contribute to the improvement?

4.1 Experimental Setup

Models and data.

Uniform CWM, APA-CWM, and LPA-CWM share the same frozen predictor, intervention generator, and cached initial responses. They differ only in candidate weighting and use the same localization and paired re-evaluation procedure. We fix M=10M=10, use one paired re-evaluation (R=1R=1), set βπ=200\beta_{\pi}=200, and apply two windowed localization updates. Only the 3.0M-parameter LPA is trained on MOVi-F trajectories, with videos split before query sampling and checkpoint selection performed on held-out MOVi-F videos. We evaluate on 30 videos each from DAVIS (Pont-Tuset et al., 2017) and Kinetics (Kay et al., 2017), using TAP-Vid point tracks and visibility annotations (Doersch et al., 2022). The same evaluation videos and queries are used for all methods; further protocol details are provided in Appendix B. RoboCOIN (Wu et al., 2025) and RoboTAP (Vecerik et al., 2024) are additionally used for qualitative manipulation examples.

Evaluation and comparisons.

We evaluate motion recovery using our CMC protocol and the standard TAP-Vid First protocol. External baselines include SMURF, GMRW, DODUO, CoTracker3, RAFT, and SEA-RAFT, covering optical flow, correspondence, and dedicated point tracking. All methods receive identical evaluation frames and queries, and no baseline uses post-hoc smoothing or repair. Appendix D describes the flow and correspondence adapters.

4.2 Completeness-aware Motion Correspondence

CMC evaluates post-query motion on ground-truth dynamic tracks. We retain tracks with at least 4 pixels of cumulative post-query displacement at 256×256256\times 256 resolution and count missing predictions on ground-truth-visible points as failures. CMC organizes its metrics into four diagnostic dimensions. Localization is summarized by DCAavg, which averages visible-and-correct predictions over {1,2,4,8,16}\{1,2,4,8,16\}-pixel thresholds. Completeness is measured by Coverage and Complete@0.8, visibility by VisBA and occlusion F1, and continuity by LCC, the longest uninterrupted predicted-visible run. Figure 4 shows one representative metric from each dimension, while Table 1 reports the full set. CTS@(4,0.8) is an additional track-level success measure requiring at least 80% coverage and mean EPE at most 4 pixels on jointly visible points. Full definitions, threshold sweeps, and fragmentation diagnostics appear in Appendix C.

We evaluate all methods under CMC on DAVIS and Kinetics (Table 1). Within the CWM family, LPA-CWM improves every reported metric over Uniform CWM and APA-CWM on both datasets. On DAVIS, CoTracker3 remains stronger in localization and several visibility-related measures, while LPA-CWM gives the strongest completeness and continuity results. On Kinetics, LPA-CWM achieves the best value among all evaluated methods on every main-paper CMC metric. Relative to Uniform CWM, learned adjudication improves DCAavg by 60.0% on DAVIS and 29.0% on Kinetics.

4.3 TAP-Vid First and Qualitative Results

TAP-Vid First is a standard evaluation protocol from TAP-Vid that queries each point at its first visible frame and evaluates the subsequent trajectory (Doersch et al., 2022). Within the CWM family, LPA-CWM achieves the best result on all five reported measures on both DAVIS and Kinetics (Table 2), consistently improving over Uniform CWM and APA-CWM. External trackers provide an additional reference under this conventional tracking protocol; CoTracker3 remains stronger on several measures, particularly on DAVIS. Together with the CMC results, these comparisons show that learned candidate weighting improves both conventional tracking accuracy and the completeness of motion recovered from the frozen CWM.

Figure 5 provides four qualitative comparisons, including a manipulation case together with human-action and animal-motion scenes. LPA-CWM gives the lowest displayed mean EPE in each example and remains stable under large motion and appearance changes. Additional qualitative results are provided in Appendix Figure F.1.

4.4 Ablation Studies

Mask count and re-evaluation.

We select MM and RR using 40 fixed query groups from 10 MOVi-F videos, with nested masks and shared queries. The sweep over M∈{5,10,20}M\in\{5,10,20\} and R∈{0,1,2}R\in\{0,1,2\} selects M=10,R=1M=10,R=1 as the best accuracy–cost setting. Increasing to 20 masks increases latency without improving endpoint accuracy, while a second re-evaluation provides no further reduction in EPE. This indicates that moderate candidate diversity together with a single refinement step is sufficient in our setting. Appendix Figure E.1 reports the full sweep and timing results.

Architecture, objectives, and decoding.

Table 3 isolates the main design choices under matched inference settings. Removing candidate-set interaction or visual cues consistently reduces performance, showing that both candidate comparison and visual context contribute to localization. For supervision, adding either coordinate or best-candidate guidance improves over KL matching alone, while the full objective performs best across all five measures. Windowed localization also improves each weighting rule, with the largest gain obtained by LPA. These results suggest that the gains come from several complementary components rather than a single design choice. Detailed controls are provided in Appendix E.

Candidate weighting.

Figure 6 examines the learned weighting before localization and re-evaluation. LPA substantially reduces candidate-space EPE and approaches the best-of-10 oracle, closing most of the gap from uniform weighting. It also assigns progressively larger weights to better candidates and more than doubles APA’s top-1 best-candidate hit rate. The learned distribution remains soft instead of collapsing to a single candidate. These results directly support the intended role of LPA: learning which CWM responses should contribute most strongly to the final motion.

5 Conclusion and Limitations

We presented LPA-CWM for improving motion reasoning with a frozen counterfactual world model. LPA learns relative reliability across competing CWM candidates from dense trajectory supervision, while APA-CWM provides a training-free analytic reference based on NSG. We also introduced CMC to evaluate localization, trajectory completeness, visibility, and continuity on dynamic tracks. Across DAVIS and Kinetics, LPA-CWM consistently improves over Uniform CWM and APA-CWM under both CMC and TAP-Vid First, while the ablations confirm the contributions of candidate interaction, trajectory supervision, and windowed localization.

Three limitations remain. First, LPA can only reweight motion evidence already present in the frozen candidate set, so missing or consistently incorrect candidates cannot be recovered; improving candidate generation or jointly adapting the underlying CWM may address this limitation. Second, LPA is trained on synthetic MOVi-F trajectories, while the current quantitative evaluation covers DAVIS and Kinetics within one CWM family. Extending trajectory supervision to real and embodied data and evaluating across additional datasets and world-model architectures will better establish generalization. Third, multi-mask inference and paired re-evaluation increase per-query computation. More efficient candidate selection, shared computation across masks, and reducing the number of required CWM evaluations are promising directions for lowering this cost.

Appendix A Implementation Details

Frozen candidate generator.

The counterfactual predictor and intervention generator remain fixed during LPA training and inference. CWM uses a 32×3232\times 32 patch-grid mask at the 256×256256\times 256 input resolution, where each mask element corresponds to one 8×88\times 8-pixel image patch; approximately 89.9% of the target-frame patch grid is hidden. Each mask-conditioned counterfactual response is evaluated on a 256×256256\times 256 response grid, and its candidate endpoint is obtained from the peak of the channel-reduced absolute RGB response. Averaging rather than summing over RGB channels changes only a constant factor and therefore does not change the peak location.

LPA architecture.

The complete LPA module contains 3,000,257 trainable parameters. The main text uses height–width–channel notation, whereas the PyTorch implementation stores image-like tensors in channel-first format. The local candidate encoder therefore receives a 10×32×3210\times 32\times 32 tensor and applies four 3×33\times 3 convolutional blocks with stride 2 and padding 1, using channel dimensions 10→32→64→128→19210\rightarrow 32\rightarrow 64\rightarrow 128\rightarrow 192. Each block uses GroupNorm and GELU, followed by global average pooling to produce a 192-dimensional local feature.

The global response encoder receives the complete normalized single-channel response in 1×32×321\times 32\times 32 format. It uses four stride-2 convolutional blocks with channel dimensions 1→16→32→64→961\rightarrow 16\rightarrow 32\rightarrow 64\rightarrow 96, with 3×33\times 3 kernels, padding 1, GroupNorm, and GELU, followed by global average pooling to produce a 96-dimensional feature. The shared frame-pair encoder receives the concatenated source and target RGB frames in 6×64×646\times 64\times 64 format and uses four analogous blocks with channel dimensions 6→32→64→128→1926\rightarrow 32\rightarrow 64\rightarrow 128\rightarrow 192, producing a 192-dimensional shared context feature.

The scalar encoder maps the 16-dimensional candidate descriptor through an MLP with dimensions 16→64→6416\rightarrow 64\rightarrow 64, followed by GELU and LayerNorm, to obtain a 64-dimensional feature. The four branches are concatenated into a 544-dimensional representation and projected by Linear(544,256)(544,256), LayerNorm, and GELU to form a 256-dimensional candidate token. The set encoder contains four pre-normalized Transformer layers with eight attention heads, a 512-dimensional feed-forward block, dropout 0.1, and GELU activation. No candidate-order positional embedding is used. The shared scoring head applies LayerNorm(256)(256), Linear(256,128)(256,128), GELU, and Linear(128,1)(128,1), followed by a softmax over the candidate dimension.

Candidate statistics.

The scalar branch receives the 16-dimensional descriptor listed in Table A.1. These statistics complement the learned visual and response encoders with compact information about displacement, response concentration, ambiguity, photometric change, and local edge structure.

Dimensions 3–10 first undergo signed-log compression. All 16 dimensions are then standardized using population means and standard deviations computed over all candidate rows in the MOVi-F training split; the same normalization statistics are stored with the checkpoint and reused at inference. Candidate-centered scalar statistics use the rounded and image-clipped candidate endpoint. Local windows are clipped to valid image support without padding, and local means are normalized by the number of valid pixels.

Local patch sampling.

Each local visual patch is centered at the source query or candidate endpoint, covers a continuous 64×6464\times 64 spatial extent, and is sampled directly onto a 32×3232\times 32 bilinear grid. If the sampling region extends beyond the image domain, out-of-bound values use border replication; candidate centers are neither discarded nor recentered.

MOVi-F training correspondence filtering.

Training samples are drawn from adjacent frames in the official MOVi-F training split using the native 128×128128\times 128 dense ground-truth forward and backward flow fields. For a native-resolution source point 𝐩\mathbf{p}, let

𝐪=𝐩+𝐅t→t+1​(𝐩).\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{F}_{t\rightarrow t+1}(\mathbf{p}).

The backward field is read at the rounded target coordinate, without bilinear interpolation, and the forward–backward consistency error is

efb​(𝐩)=‖𝐅t→t+1​(𝐩)+𝐁t+1→t​(round⁡(𝐪))‖2.e_{\mathrm{fb}}(\mathbf{p})=\left\|\mathbf{F}_{t\rightarrow t+1}(\mathbf{p})+\mathbf{B}_{t+1\rightarrow t}\left(\operatorname{round}(\mathbf{q})\right)\right\|_{2}.

A correspondence is retained only when efb≤2.0e_{\mathrm{fb}}\leq 2.0 pixels at the native 128×128128\times 128 resolution and both the source and warped target are at least four pixels from the image boundary. Out-of-frame targets, points too close to the boundary, and non-finite consistency errors are discarded rather than clamped back into the valid domain. The sampling procedure additionally requires a minimum moving magnitude of 0.25 pixels at the native resolution. Accepted frames and coordinates are subsequently mapped to the common 256×256256\times 256 training scale.

LPA training.

MOVi-F is partitioned at the source-video level before frame-pair and query sampling, and each training sample retains the complete M=10M=10 candidate set. Candidate order is randomly permuted during training. AdamW uses a learning rate of 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, batch size 16, and a cosine schedule. Checkpoint selection uses candidate-space weighted-coordinate EPE on held-out MOVi-F validation videos. This criterion corresponds to the weighted-coordinate supervision in Section 3.3 and is distinct from the final deployed endpoint EPE reported in the MM–RR configuration study.

Analytic precursor.

APA-CWM uses a frozen Ablated Diffusion Model (ADM) score network with approximately 552M parameters, evaluated in FP16 at 224×224224\times 224 resolution and diffusion time ts=0.006t_{s}=0.006. The score map PP is computed once per frame pair using the same numerical stabilizer 10−610^{-6} as in the main text and bilinearly resampled to the 256×256256\times 256 CWM response grid. APA averages the aligned statistic within a radius-six neighborhood around each candidate response peak, clips the candidate values to [10−3,103][10^{-3},10^{3}], and applies L1 normalization across candidates. The score map is used only by APA-CWM; LPA-CWM does not consume the diffusion score map.

Counterfactual decoding.

For each frame pair and query, MM denotes the number of mask-conditioned candidate responses in the initial CWM set, whereas RR denotes the number of paired re-evaluation passes after the initial localization. The two hyperparameters therefore control different stages of inference.

When R=0R=0, only the initial candidate set is weighted and localized, with no additional CWM pass. For the default R=1R=1, the decoder-specific initial endpoint conditions one coarse-conditioned paired re-evaluation. The source location remains the original query, while the initial endpoint determines the center of the heuristic masking applied to the target frame. At 256×256256\times 256 resolution, both source and target retain complete spatial support. A fresh set of MM masks is sampled, and the frozen CWM recomputes MM mask-conditioned responses. APA and LPA are not rerun, the initial candidate weights are not reused, and the fresh responses are uniformly aggregated. The discrete peak of the resulting response distribution gives the refined endpoint. Thus, the default R=1R=1 stage is a full-field coarse-conditioned paired re-evaluation rather than a local crop refinement.

For R>1R>1, later passes may become progressively local. The crop side follows sr=s1​ηr−1s_{r}=s_{1}\eta^{r-1} with fixed η=0.75\eta=0.75; η\eta changes only the crop size and is neither learned nor used in candidate weighting. For non-square inputs, the first square crop uses the shorter image dimension and is shifted to remain inside the valid image region rather than padded.

Standard and windowed localization.

Both decoders start from the same aggregated response distribution using the softmax inverse-temperature parameter βπ=200\beta_{\pi}=200. Standard localization applies no Gaussian-window update and passes the discrete argmax of the unwindowed response distribution to the subsequent RR stage. Windowed localization performs two Gaussian-window reweighting steps. At each step, the continuous distribution mean and spatial standard deviation determine the window center and scale, with width 3​max⁡(σ,0.5)3\max(\sigma,0.5); the distribution is renormalized after each update. The coordinate passed to the RR stage is the discrete argmax after the second update, not the continuous expectation. The two window updates operate within a fixed response field and are distinct from the paired CWM re-evaluation passes.

Trajectory construction.

For each adjacent frame pair, the refined endpoint predicted for the current query is used as the source query in the next pair. The complete post-query trajectory is constructed before any CMC metric is computed. LPA-CWM inherits the CWM response-strength visibility signal and does not train a separate visibility or occlusion head. All compared methods use the same sampled frame sequence, image coordinates, and query identities.

Appendix B Datasets and Evaluation Protocols

Evaluation datasets.

We evaluate on TAP-Vid DAVIS and TAP-Vid Kinetics (Doersch et al., 2022), which provide human-annotated point tracks and visibility labels for object-centric and in-the-wild videos, respectively. DAVIS contains challenging deformation, occlusion, distractors, and fast motion (Pont-Tuset et al., 2017), whereas Kinetics-400 introduces broader variation in actions, camera motion, viewpoint, and human–object interaction (Kay et al., 2017). We use fixed evaluation subsets and identical sampled frames and query tracks for all methods. No model parameter is adapted to either evaluation dataset.

Evaluation protocol.

Following the TAP-Vid First protocol (Doersch et al., 2022), each query is introduced at its first visible frame and evaluated on subsequent frames. Ground-truth coordinates and visibility are taken directly from the TAP-Vid annotations. The same query sets are used for Uniform CWM, APA-CWM, LPA-CWM, and all external baselines, and missing predictions on annotated visible points are retained as failures rather than removed from evaluation. The CWM variants also share the same cached initial response sets; only their candidate weighting differs before the common localization and paired re-evaluation procedure.

TAP-Vid metrics.

We report Average Jaccard, points within the benchmark distance thresholds, mean and median endpoint distance, and occlusion accuracy. Average Jaccard jointly reflects localization and visibility, while the distance metrics separately summarize typical and tail localization errors. CMC uses the same ground-truth tracks but evaluates motion correspondence from the complementary perspectives of localization, completeness, visibility, and temporal continuity, as detailed in Appendix C.

Appendix C Completeness-aware Motion Correspondence

We introduce Completeness-aware Motion Correspondence (CMC) to evaluate motion correspondence on ground-truth dynamic tracks while explicitly penalizing incomplete predictions. Dynamic tracks are selected from ground truth, and missing visible-point predictions remain in the accuracy denominator.

For both datasets, the ground-truth coordinates and visibility labels are read directly from TAP-Vid point-track annotations. We use TAP-Vid DAVIS point tracks for the DAVIS videos and TAP-Vid Kinetics point tracks for the Kinetics videos; DAVIS segmentation annotations are not converted into trajectories (Doersch et al., 2022).

Let qiq_{i} be the query frame of trajectory ii, xi,tgtx^{\rm gt}_{i,t} and x^i,t\hat{x}_{i,t} the ground-truth and predicted coordinates, and vi,tgt,v^i,t∈{0,1}v^{\rm gt}_{i,t},\hat{v}_{i,t}\in\{0,1\} their visibility labels. Only post-query, ground-truth-visible frames are evaluated:

Ei={t:t>qi,vi,tgt=1}.E_{i}=\{t:t>q_{i},\ v^{\rm gt}_{i,t}=1\}.

The post-query ground-truth path length is

Li,>qgt=∑t≥qi𝟏[vi,tgt=vi,t+1gt=1]∥xi,t+1gt−xi,tgt∥2.L^{\rm gt}_{i,>q}=\sum_{t\geq q_{i}}\mathbf{1}[v^{\rm gt}_{i,t}=v^{\rm gt}_{i,t+1}=1]\lVert x^{\rm gt}_{i,t+1}-x^{\rm gt}_{i,t}\rVert_{2}.

The dynamic set 𝒟={i:Li,>qgt≥4}\mathcal{D}=\{i:L^{\rm gt}_{i,>q}\geq 4\} is defined on a common 256-pixel coordinate scale and is independent of all predictions.

Completeness.

Per-track visibility coverage and its thresholded counterpart are

Ci=∑t∈Ei𝟏[v^i,t=1]|Ei|,Coverage=1|𝒟|​∑i∈𝒟Ci,C_{i}=\frac{\sum_{t\in E_{i}}\mathbf{1}[\hat{v}_{i,t}=1]}{|E_{i}|},\qquad\mathrm{Coverage}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}C_{i},
Complete@0.8=1|𝒟|∑i∈𝒟𝟏[Ci≥0.8].\mathrm{Complete@0.8}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}\mathbf{1}[C_{i}\geq 0.8].

These are completeness diagnostics, not localization-accuracy measures.

Dynamic Correspondence Accuracy.

With ei,t=∥x^i,t−xi,tgt∥2e_{i,t}=\lVert\hat{x}_{i,t}-x^{\rm gt}_{i,t}\rVert_{2}, we define

DCAτ=∑i∈𝒟∑t∈Ei𝟏[v^i,t=1]𝟏[ei,t<τ]∑i∈𝒟|Ei|.\mathrm{DCA}_{\tau}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}\sum_{t\in E_{i}}\mathbf{1}[\hat{v}_{i,t}=1]\mathbf{1}[e_{i,t}<\tau]}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}|E_{i}|}.

Thus a prediction marked invisible contributes zero rather than disappearing from the denominator. The primary scalar summary is

DCAavg=15​∑τ∈{1,2,4,8,16}DCAτ.\mathrm{DCA}_{\rm avg}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{\tau\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}}\mathrm{DCA}_{\tau}.

Complete Track Success.

Let e¯ijoint\bar{e}_{i}^{\rm joint} be the mean EPE over frames in EiE_{i} that are also predicted visible. The track-level criterion is

CTS(τ,c)=1|𝒟|∑i∈𝒟𝟏[Ci≥c]𝟏[e¯ijoint≤τ].\mathrm{CTS}(\tau,c)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}\mathbf{1}[C_{i}\geq c]\mathbf{1}[\bar{e}_{i}^{\rm joint}\leq\tau].

We report CTS@(4,0.8) and CTS@(8,0.8). CTS is secondary to DCA because it still allows up to 20% of a track to be absent.

Visibility and continuity.

Visibility balanced accuracy is

VisBA=12​(TPRvisible+TNRoccluded),\mathrm{VisBA}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathrm{TPR}_{\rm visible}+\mathrm{TNR}_{\rm occluded}),

and occlusion F1 is computed from post-query occlusion labels. For each ground-truth-visible segment, longest continuous coverage (LCC) is the longest predicted-visible run divided by |Ei||E_{i}|. Fragmentation counts the number of →→11\!\rightarrow\!0\!\rightarrow\!1 visibility recoveries within such segments; Table C.2 reports the mean count.

Threshold sensitivity.

Figure C.1 evaluates whether the CMC conclusions depend on the default dynamic-motion and coverage thresholds. With the coverage threshold fixed at c=0.8c=0.8, we vary the ground-truth motion threshold Lmotion∈{2,4,8}L_{\rm motion}\in\{2,4,8\} pixels and report DCAavg. LPA-CWM changes only from 59.42 to 58.30 across this range and remains above APA-CWM and Uniform CWM at every setting. We then fix Lmotion=4L_{\rm motion}=4 pixels and vary the coverage threshold c∈{0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9}c\in\{0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9\} for CTS@(4,cc). LPA-CWM remains best throughout, decreasing moderately from 58.79 to 56.29 as the coverage requirement becomes stricter. The method ordering is therefore stable around the default Lmotion=4L_{\rm motion}=4 pixels and c=0.8c=0.8.

Appendix D Adapting External Estimators

Coordinates.

CoTracker3 is evaluated with the official offline point-tracking interface: the full video and first-visible query are provided jointly, and the predictor returns the complete trajectory directly. It therefore requires neither a flow-to-coordinate adapter nor recursive flow propagation. RAFT, SEA-RAFT, DODUO, and SMURF instead predict each post-query coordinate directly from the original query frame. For a query introduced at frame qq, each query–target pair (Iq,It)(I_{q},I_{t}) for t>qt>q is evaluated independently, and the forward displacement at the original query location gives the target coordinate. Reverse predictions, when computed, are used only for visibility estimation. GMRW uses its official tracking utility to propagate correspondences through adjacent frames.

Visibility.

Table D.1 summarizes the visibility rules used by the external estimators. CoTracker3 uses the Boolean visibility returned by its official offline predictor, which thresholds the native visibility score at 0.9 and forces the annotated query point to be visible. No additional forward–backward consistency test is applied.

For the flow and correspondence estimators, out-of-frame or non-finite predictions are treated as invisible by the corresponding adapters. CoTracker3 retains the native visibility returned by the official predictor without an additional out-of-frame, non-finite, or forward–backward filter. These evaluation-time visibility rules are distinct from the ground-truth forward–backward filtering used to construct MOVi-F training samples in Appendix A.

Aggregation.

All metrics are first computed from the same per-video query set and then aggregated with equal video weight. No point or video is selected using a method’s predicted error, coverage, or visibility. Missing predictions enter DCA as failures.

Appendix E Ablation Protocols

Joint MM–RR sensitivity.

The audit uses 40 query groups from 10 held-out MOVi-F videos, shared across configurations. We evaluate M∈{5,10,20}×R∈{0,1,2}M\in\{5,10,20\}\times R\in\{0,1,2\}. Masks are nested prefixes of the same ordered 20-mask set, avoiding independent draws for smaller MM. All runs use full LPA-CWM on identical videos, frame pairs, and queries. We report final endpoint EPE after localization and RR paired re-evaluations. The sweep selects M=10,R=1M=10,R=1 for the main comparison.

Latency measurement.

Figure E.1 uses a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 with batch size 1, where each timed sample contains one adjacent frame pair and one query group. CUDA is synchronized immediately before and after the complete model call. Timing includes the factual frozen-CWM forward pass, MM mask-conditioned counterfactual evaluations, LPA feature extraction and set processing, candidate aggregation, localization, the specified RR paired CWM re-evaluation passes, and final endpoint extraction. Disk I/O, CPU preprocessing, host-to-device transfer, and model or checkpoint initialization are excluded. We therefore report end-to-end per-query latency under this protocol rather than throughput-optimized peak speed.

Candidate-weight analysis.

Candidates are ranked within each complete ten-candidate group by ground-truth endpoint EPE. The top-1 oracle hit rate measures how often the highest-weight candidate is the minimum-EPE candidate. Effective support is exp(−∑mwmlogwm)\exp(-\sum_{m}w_{m}\log w_{m}): it equals 1 for one-hot weights and 10 for uniform weights. Figure 6 reports video-macro summaries. This analysis uses the MOVi-F validation split used for checkpoint selection and serves as mechanism evidence; real-video tracking is evaluated separately.

EPE definitions across analyses.

Figure E.1 evaluates 40 fixed query groups using the final deployed endpoint after localization and the requested RR re-evaluation passes; the default M=10,R=1M=10,R=1 setting obtains 2.1363 pixels. Figure 6 instead evaluates 640 complete M=10M=10 candidate groups using the candidate-space weighted-coordinate surrogate before response-level localization and paired re-evaluation, where LPA obtains 2.41 pixels. These values are not directly comparable because they use different validation subsets and endpoint definitions.

Inference-stage ablation.

All six configurations use the same frozen CWM, M=10M=10, R=1R=1, evaluation seed, DAVIS batches, frame pairs, queries, and initial masks. The rows are Uniform + Std., APA + Std., Uniform + Win., APA + Win., LPA + Std., and LPA + Win.. “Std.” uses the discrete peak of the unwindowed aggregated response distribution as the initial endpoint. “Win.” applies two Gaussian-window reweighting updates and uses the discrete peak of the final distribution. Uniform, APA, and LPA respectively denote equal, analytic, and learned weights for the initial candidate set. All six rows then use the same one-pass coarse-conditioned paired re-evaluation after their decoder-specific initial endpoint. The second pass does not rerun APA or LPA, does not reuse the initial weights, and uniformly aggregates the freshly generated responses. This 3×23\times 2 design therefore separates initial candidate weighting from localization.

Learned architecture and objective ablations.

Architecture variants use the complete three-term objective, the same windowed localization, and the same R=1R=1 paired re-evaluation. “w/o candidate-set interaction” removes the permutation-equivariant set Transformer, while “response + scalar cues only” removes the local RGB and shared frame-pair raw encoders but retains response maps, 16 scalar statistics, and candidate-set interaction. Objective variants retain the full LPA architecture and compare ℒKL\mathcal{L}_{\rm KL}, ℒKL+ℒcoord\mathcal{L}_{\rm KL}+\mathcal{L}_{\rm coord}, ℒKL+ℒbest\mathcal{L}_{\rm KL}+\mathcal{L}_{\rm best}, and the full three-term objective. Table 3 reports every row under the TAP-Vid First protocol on the same DAVIS evaluation set and cached initial CWM candidate responses. Its five columns are TAP-Vid localization and occlusion measures. The inference procedure is fixed except for the named architecture or objective component.
